chapter: Reel 2: Perez, brass bands and early life
title: Manuel Perez, the wah-wah mute and Chicago
summary: Ferbos says Perez may have been first with the wah-wah mute, could improvise, and carried above the street band; he later worked in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: One thing I want to ask you about, and that's something I've never been able to get straight in my head. You say Manuel Perez used a wah-wah mute, huh?

He used to, uh, yeah, he used to, from what I can understand, he was the first one that did that. And when he went to Chicago, then quite a few fellas picked it up up there after that. Now, if it's actually, he originated or not, I mean, I don't know, but it's only, maybe it's only his seat. I don't know.
Well now, could he get off? Could he get away from the melody much?

Oh yeah, he could, he could improvise, yeah. Oh yeah, he could improvise. And he was a good street man too. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. He could play above all those instruments. You could hear him coming down the street above all those instruments.
Would he play in a ratty, tonk style if he wanted to? He could do that, huh? Yeah, he could improvise, yeah. And he could play the regular street music, the legit style too.
Yeah, because then he went to Chicago, he worked in the theater office for a long time. But he could play, because he used to play dances, I mean, and he'd play all that stuff.
